Where it began

Michael Vaughan was born on 29 October 1974 in Eccles, near Manchester, and cricket was already in the family tree: Ernest and Johnny Tyldesley, who played for Lancashire and England early in the twentieth century, were his great-great-uncles. When he was nine the family moved to Sheffield, and he grew up there as keen on football as on cricket.

It was the cricket that found him. Playing for his school, he caught the eye of the Yorkshire coach Doug Padgett. There was one snag. In those days Yorkshire picked only men born in the county, and Eccles is not in Yorkshire. When that rule went, Padgett came back for him, and Vaughan joined the Yorkshire academy. He was a professional at 17 and captained England Under-19s in 1993 and 1994.

The player

A right-handed batter who often opened, alongside Marcus Trescothick, Vaughan played 82 Tests for England between 1999 and 2008. He made 5,719 runs at 41.44, with 18 hundreds and a best of 197 against India at Trent Bridge.

His debut, in South Africa in November 1999, was a baptism: he walked in at two for two, it soon became four for two, and he calmly made 33. His great run came in 2002 and the winter that followed. He scored 1,481 Test runs in that calendar year, then made 633 in the Ashes in Australia, with 177 at Adelaide, 145 at Melbourne and 183 at Sydney. For a while he was ranked the best batter in the world.

What made him special

Made captain in 2003, he turned England into a side that expected to win. In 2004 they won eleven Tests and lost none, and in 2005 they beat Australia 2–1 to take the Ashes for the first time in 18 years. His 166 at Old Trafford was his best innings of that summer. In all he led England in 51 Tests and won 26, at the time more than any other England captain.

One-day cricket was the one stage that never quite suited him. In 86 matches he got as close as 90 not out against Zimbabwe, but the hundred never came, which only proves that even the classiest players have one door that stays stubbornly shut.

Away from the middle

After the Ashes he was made an OBE and given the freedom of Sheffield, and he received an honorary doctorate from Sheffield Hallam University. In 2003 he was a Wisden Cricketer of the Year and the first player ever to appear on the almanack's cover.

He left the game in June 2009 and moved into broadcasting, on Test Match Special and on television in England and Australia. He wrote three books about his career, carried the Olympic torch through Hillingdon in 2012, and that same year danced on Strictly Come Dancing.

And finally

In retirement he found an unusual way to paint: hitting cricket balls at a wall. For a man who once spent a whole Ashes summer doing much the same thing to Australian bowling, it must have felt like familiar work.
